title: The Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment, a 1932–1972 US Public Health Service study that observed roughly 400 Black men with late-stage syphilis in Macon County, Alabama, without treating them, while they believed they were receiving "special free treatment." The episode covers syphilis's history and stages, how the study began and was run (placebos, spinal taps, draft exemptions, penicillin being withheld), whistleblowers such as Peter Buxton and Bill Jenkins, the 1972 AP story that ended the study, congressional hearings, the lawsuit settlement and health benefits, the resulting informed-consent and research ethics reforms (National Research Act, Belmont Report), the related Guatemala syphilis experiments, and the lasting "Tuskegee effect" on trust in medicine. Ends with a call for listeners to share the show.
topics: Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male

segments.title: Introduction and overview of the study
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Tuskegee study, a listener recommendation from Miles Kendrick, its official name, and the basic facts: Black men in Macon County, Alabama with syphilis were left untreated for decades, believing they were being treated for bad blood. Covers the study's stated reasons and the misconception that participants were infected by the researchers.

segments.title: Why Macon County and the study's origins
segments.summary: The men were poor sharecroppers chosen for vulnerability and high syphilis prevalence in Macon County. The study began in 1932 after a funded treatment program ran out of money, and the researchers chose not to treat. Also covers the 1927 Alabama law requiring syphilis treatment being ignored, and participants being lured with hot meals, treatment and burial insurance.

segments.title: Syphilis history and disease stages
segments.summary: Explains syphilis as a bacterial infection (Treponema pallidum) with origins traced to Naples in 1495, its spread through Europe and Asia, possible Columbus-era origin hypothesis, and its stages including latency, organ damage, blindness, deafness, and neurological effects. Notes most study men were in late latency.

segments.title: Recruitment and Eunice Rivers
segments.summary: The study enrolled 399 infected men and 201 controls. Nurse Eunice Rivers helped recruit participants through word of mouth and churches, was co-author on two of the thirteen papers, and was vilified; she believed the Public Health Service's claims about racial differences.

segments.title: Penicillin withheld and the draft exemption
segments.summary: Describes earlier syphilis treatments (mercury, arsphenamine) and penicillin's proven cure, including its 1940 publication, while the study continued withholding it. Researchers blocked participants from getting penicillin elsewhere, and in World War II exempted them from the draft to avoid STD testing and treatment; the director of public health for Macon County helped arrange this.

segments.title: Study launch, Oslo comparison, and deception tactics
segments.summary: Study launched by Taliaferro Clark of the Venereal Disease Division, a two-arm study. Oslo study of white men (1891–1910, published 1929) was used as comparison. Tuskegee Institute's link is discussed. Participants were told they got 'special free treatment' with placebos such as aspirin and tonics. Raymond Vonderlehr took over in 1934 and added dangerous spinal taps.

segments.title: Nuremberg, ongoing excuses, and early dissent
segments.summary: The study continued after the Nuremberg Trials. Researchers persisted in the excuse that treating late syphilis was harmful, which was outdated after penicillin. Cutler's 1993 remarks defended withholding penicillin. Surgeon General certificates were given in 1957.

segments.title: Early critics: Count Gibson, Bill Jenkins, Irwin Schatz
segments.summary: Early critics included Richmond physician Count Gibson, who was silenced by his medical college; CDC statistician Bill Jenkins, who tried to get the New York Times and Washington Post to cover it; and Detroit cardiologist Irwin Schatz, who urged reevaluation of moral judgments.

segments.title: Peter Buxton and the 1972 AP story
segments.summary: Peter Buxton, a Public Health Service venereal disease investigator in San Francisco, found the study in 1965, confronted William J. Brown, and was ignored. He sent files to the AP; reporter Gene Heller's 1972 article ran in newspapers including the New York Times, causing public outrage.

segments.title: Hearings, study end, and compensation
segments.summary: Senator Edward M. Kennedy called congressional hearings. An advisory panel said the study was ethically unjustified. The study was poorly run, and about 128 men died from untreated syphilis. In 1997 President Clinton apologized to survivors; a settlement provided payments and the Tuskegee Health Benefit Program provided medical care from 1975.

segments.title: The Tuskegee effect and medical distrust
segments.summary: Families were at risk of infection. Studies show the Tuskegee study reduced Black men's medical care use by 22 percent in the following years and increased distrust, including in the AIDS era. Historian Susan Reverby notes structural racism continues.

segments.title: Reforms: informed consent, National Research Act, Belmont Report
segments.summary: After 1972, Congress and NIH changed rules requiring informed consent and peer review of study design. The National Research Act passed in 1974. The US adopted informed consent late relative to the 1947 Nuremberg Code. The 1979 Belmont Report set principles of respect, beneficence and justice, adopted in 1995.

segments.title: Guatemala syphilis experiments
segments.summary: The US-funded Guatemala experiments (1946–1948) deliberately infected soldiers, prisoners, sex workers and mental patients with syphilis. Doctor John Charles Cutler ran them and had earlier done similar work in prisons. Three patients died and about 700 received minimal treatment.

segments.title: Structural racism and ER pain medication study
segments.summary: A 2020 Oregon emergency room study found Black patients were less likely to be given pain medication than white patients despite similar pain scores. Hosts discuss the need to teach this history.

segments.title: Listener call to share the show
segments.summary: Instead of listener mail, Chuck asks listeners to share their favorite episode with three friends to help grow the show.
